The reason we coined the new word "electronic", when we already had the word "electric", was that we needed a way to refer to electrical components (other than batteries) whose functioning depended on the fact that the most mobile carriers of electrical charge were electrons -- vacuum tubes, whose thermionic effect depended on electrons being lighter particles, and n/p junctions, whose voltage-dependent resistance depended on electrons being subject to quantum effects. replies.title: (no subject)
replies.content:
Belief need not be in the form of "I believe that X is the sole objective truth." It can also be in the form of "I believe that X is a working approximation of the truth," or even "I have no idea what the truth is, but I believe that X works."

From some perspectives, thinking that any one system is "the ultimate way" is by definition a delusion, and an egotistical delusion at that. Nor is it especially useful -- any benefit you get in terms of focus and emotional comfort is paid for in terms of narrowness and lack of compassion.

Do you recall the story about Socrates and the Delphic oracle? The oracle announced once that Socrates was the wisest man in Greece. He was baffled by this, since everyone around him seemed to be sure that they knew this or that, while he realized that he didn't really know anything. Finally it sank in that he was the wisest man in Greece because none of them actually knew anything, but he alone realized this.

I would have used "magical" for that latter sense. Complex systems science (along with computer science, and statistics and computational statistics and computational cognitive science and decision theory and algorithmic probability theory, and computational science and the calculational parts of physics, and in a sense all of mathematics) just *is* deeper realities, even if it's only some of them. So there's no contradiction between that and a partial program of deep contemplative occult training, that ties together phenomena on basically all levels accessible to materialist awareness. It even syncretizes okay with the Taoist scheme of five elements. Complex systems science is definitely the centerpiece I would go for, if I was designing such a thing.

Maybe the thing that Dion Fortune figured by the term "initiation of the nadir" is even a real thing, that's substantially *about* The Powers That Be getting people to do some minimal amount of "occult training" where they get a minimal semi-conscious practical grasp of complex systems effects, in the way that those effects would have (in principle) applied to (say) a human life even in a non-teleological materialist universe.

To do something parallel to the Western thing where you pathwork the elemental realms, perhaps you'd need the seeker to practice some simplified version of multigrid finite-element calculations by hand. They could notice things like how solid bodies are easier to simulate when you formulate the physical question in terms of Lagrangian comoving coordinates, while fluids sometimes do better with with the coordinates Eulerian / fixed-coordinates-with-transiting-materials formulation, and for fire you'd need to be tracking distributions of velocities of a variety of simple and compound particles and molecules. Perhaps animating them by hand and checking for plausibility in the resulting motions would also work. Or they could notice how intense vibrations are bounced in nonlinear ways by solid materials in locally consistent ways, that require one to build up a local understanding of how each part responds and let that understanding amortize over multiple calculations, whereas in fluid materials it's more a matter of learning the probability distribution of what the fluid flow state would have been at the moment and doing a lot of fudging since the details won't matter as long as the overall random outcome is arrived at fairly. Anyway, maybe that's impractical, and also it doesn't seem like it would necessarily be enough by itself. That doesn't contain, I think, any positive elements of a program that could be used for a straightforward materialist without straying into magic, but the parts about plausible deniability and "my cosmology ate my homework" are UTTERLY FOUNDATIONAL to understanding how it psychologically and cosmologically works for us to even have been able to land on an outcome where "admitting to themselves that that's what they're doing" would even be a constraint. Another example of this kind of point of contact is the reasoning style described in https://ecosophia.dreamwidth.org/364211.html?thread=59755443#cmt59797683 .

If you give someone occult training in a materialist cosmology, and as a consequence they contact something, for the most part the things they contact will go out of their way to be readily interpretable as being nothing more than "human-universal convergent subpersonality psychological dynamical attractor-structures that coordinate their action across people through paradoxically high-bandwidth subtle variations in body language / microexpressions / pheromones / artistic common points of reference" (see https://ecosophia.dreamwidth.org/359082.html?thread=59209386#cmt59262378 ). Why listen to the traditional warnings and follow the traditional rules, if the warnings depend on supposed causal mechanisms of action that a mere psychological attractor-structure, being a mere shadow of a mind trapped inside their head, would be powerless to actuate? And then JMG describes a typical outcome at https://ecosophia.dreamwidth.org/335594.html?thread=56411626#cmt56413162 . You'd need the person to forego magic entirely, or commit to some kind of failsafe where if they started believing in magical powers they had to also switch over to believing some functional tradition's warnings about those powers.

Magical systems are sort of to occult systems what engineering is to theoretical science. You know that science fiction saying about "any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic"? I have a sort of reverse of that saying (paraphrased from another saying in software engineering): "any sufficiently advanced technology that's not already a magical system from the bottom up, but still manages to maintain its purpose, contains an ad-hoc, informally-specified, bug-ridden, inefficient implementation of half of a magical system". Any kind of purpose in a complex slippery situation might have, in some sense, the same inherent difficulties that magic has, and so might eventually have to settle on provisional approaches to solving the same kinds of internal problems that a magical system does. For example, countries have to develop systems of law and jurisprudence. See https://ecosophia.dreamwidth.org/360870.html?thread=59400102#cmt59455398 . (The link I couldn't find there about magic vs. alchemy vs. engineering vs. science was https://ecosophia.dreamwidth.org/321639.html?thread=54769255#cmt54820967 ). So that's another point of contact.

comments.title: Auspicious/Inauspicious Days and Times
comments.content:
I would like to pick your mind a bit, JMG, on the subject of days or times that are generally “good” or “bad.” I have a basic understanding of the planetary days and planetary hours in Western astrology / geomancy / occultism and the concept that initiating or engaging in a particular activity that is in harmony with the planet associated with that activity during the day and hour of that same planet is beneficial. During Shakespeare’s time, for example, May 3rd was considered to be the most unlucky/inauspicious day of the year (at least he referred to it in one of his plays – I don’t recall which one), though I have no idea why that would be so.

I ask this question because I am quite familiar with Vedic astrology and its application to daily life through what one may call an astrological almanac (called “panchang” in Sanskrit). It is a rectified lunar calendar and in it there are a few days sprinkled throughout the year which are considered to be auspicious for any activity; while in the course of each day there are auspicious time periods (such as Abhijit) and inauspicious time periods (such as Rahu kaala). I know of no such equivalent, or even similarity, between the panchang of India and the sense of good/bad timing in Western calendrical systems – but that may be due to my ignorance on the subject. What sayest thou?

Ron M

replies.title: Re: Auspicious/Inauspicious Days and Times
replies.content:
There used to be an extensive body of lore on auspicious and inauspicious days in the calendar. Each day of the lunar cycle, from the Moon's first visible appearance on, was either fortunate or unfortunate for certain things, and there were certain days of each month, called the Egyptian days, when nothing could be expected to go well. All that dropped out of popular culture in the 17th and 18th centuries. Old Western almanacs used to be very similar to the panchang, for that matter, and were strongly lunar in their focus. Have you ever heard the old English folk song "Tom o' Bedlam's Song"?

"From the hag and the hungry goblin
That into rags would rend ye,
The spirit that stands by the naked man
In the book of moons defend ye,
That by your five sound senses
Ye may not be forsaken,
Nor wander from yourselves with Tom
Abroad to beg your bacon."

As any Cabalist knows, the spirit that stands by the naked man is the archangel Gabriel, associated with Yesod, the 9th sphere of the Tree of Life, whose magical image is a naked man and which rules the Moon and therefore madness (or as we still call it, lunacy). "Book of moons" is an old term for an almanac. We have lost so much in the Western world!

It looks like there is a significant effort may be required to piece together whatever remnants we have of such systems of wisdom (and reverse engineer the rest) before the steep slope of decline puts most people into 'bare survival mode' in future generations. The alternative is for all this wisdom to be regenerated the slow, hard way - that is, from scratch - which kinda sucks.

There's a significant amount of scholarship on early almanacs, but it mostly flies under the radar of people interested in esoteric matters. Here's a partial bibliography. I was able to find all of them online somewhere or other.

George Lyman Kittredge. The Old Farmer and his Almanack. 1904.

George Emery Littlefield. “Notes on the Calendar and the Almanac.” Proceedings of the American Antiquarian Society. 1914.

Clarence S. Brigham. An Account of American Almaancs and their Value for Historical Study. 1925.

Marion Barber Stowell. Early American Almanacs: The Colonial Weekday Bible. 1976.

Bernard Capp. Astrology and the Popular Press: English Almanacs 1500–1800. 1979.

Louise Hill Curth. English Almanacs, Astrology and Popular Medicine., 1550–1700. 2007.

* Matthew J. Shaw. “Keeping Time in the Age of Franklin: Almanacs and the Atlantic World.” Printing History, vol. 2. 2007.

* T. J. Tomlin. “ ‘Astrology’s from Heaven, not from Hell’: The Religious Significance of Early American Almanacs.” Early American Studies, 2:1. 2010.

Phebe Jensen. Astrology, Almanacs, and the Early English Calendar. 2021.

[The two items marked with an asterisk * are fairly recent journal articles, not books. Those may be harder for you to access. I could perhaps upload PDFs to archive.org if you want them.]

I wrote a short popular article for a local publication, The Witches' Almanac, that may be somewhat relevant, too: "Traces of Paganism in The Maine Farmer's Almanac, 1932-1957" (in the almanac for 2012-2013). I'll put it up on archive.org tonight.

comments.title: Ritual Material Substitutes
comments.content:
Good evening JMG,

Apologies for the late question, but I was not master of the clock today. My question regards ritual materials and substitutes. I understand there are no hard and fast rules but I am looking for a philosophical approach. Dealing with the wisdom of the past and rituals and spells from earlier ages, I find it problematic gathering certain materials and wonder if others in our time have encountered this and adapted to it.

Let me give an example. A ritual to create a iynx calls for some earth from the grave of someone who died young. I imagine in ages past, this probably would not have been in all that difficult but in our time... I can definitely imagine me skulking about a cemetery after hours with a trowel getting spotlighted by the cops and having some uncomfortable explaining to do. Do you and/or others have similar issues and how have you handled this? Thank you in advance.

replies.title: Re: Ritual Material Substitutes
replies.content:
Sometimes substitutions are relatively easy; sometimes they're not. If you're working with planetary or elemental energies, for example, you can swap things out easily if you know the symbolism. Let's say you find a ritual that calls for the brains of a lion. The brain corresponds to the Moon, and the lion to Leo; find an herb that corresponds to Moon in Leo, or simply consecrate a talisman when the Moon is well dignified in Leo, and you're good.

Graveyard dirt is another matter, but it's also much easier to gather than you seem to think. There are many neglected graveyards, and even well-tended ones are pretty safe in most cases. You don't go in after hours! You simply go walking there in the usual way, a folding trowel and a ziploc bag in your pocket; when you find an appropriate grave, wait until nobody's in sight, kneel, extract a little dirt, and go your way.

In hoodoo practice, btw, it's appropriate to pay the dead person for their help. A genuine silver dime is considered appropriate, and a libation suitable to the person. For example, to complete an assignment for the hoodoo course I took, I needed graveyard dirt from the graveyard of a soldier. That was easy. There was a neglected cemetery close to where I lived at that time; it had graves of Civil War vets; the process I've just described went smoothly, and I paid for the dirt with a Mercury dime thrust into the ground and an airline bottle of decent whiskey poured on it, which the ghost seems to have appreciated. Oh, and always go back by a different route than you came.

replies.content: that's fantastic advice, many thanks.
